canonical_statement: The review evaluates major benefits, risks, and clinical implications of recent large placebo-controlled testosterone trials in middle-aged and older men with low or low-normal testosterone and no identifiable hypothalamic-pituitary-testicular pathology.

source_anchor.paragraph: Review scope paragraph

canonical_statement: The authors focused on four testosterone trials enrolling at least 300 men, using placebo controls, providing at least 1 year of therapy, and assessing clinically important outcomes.

source_anchor.paragraph: Review scope paragraph

canonical_statement: The review concerns middle-aged and older men with symptoms, signs, or end-organ features possibly attributable to androgen deficiency, low or low-normal serum testosterone, and no identifiable HPT-axis pathology.

canonical_statement: The source is a narrative review of four landmark trials rather than a systematic review, and some outcomes discussed are secondary or substudy analyses rather than primary trial outcomes.

canonical_statement: TEAAM enrolled 308 men aged at least 60 years with total testosterone 3.47-13.9 nmol/L and compared daily transdermal testosterone gel 75 mg with placebo for 3 years, adjusting dosage to maintain total testosterone 17.4-31.2 nmol/L.

exposures.details: Dose adjusted to serum total testosterone 17.4-31.2 nmol/L

canonical_statement: The T-Trials enrolled 790 men aged at least 65 years with total testosterone at or below 9.5 nmol/L plus symptoms or signs of testosterone deficiency and compared daily transdermal testosterone gel 50 mg with placebo for 1 year, titrating testosterone into the normal range.

population.label: T-Trials participants
inclusion_criteria: Symptoms or signs of testosterone deficiency

exposures.details: Dose adjusted to keep serum testosterone within the normal range

canonical_statement: T4DM enrolled 1007 men aged 50-74 years with total testosterone at or below 14 nmol/L and impaired glucose tolerance or newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, and compared intramuscular testosterone undecanoate 1000 mg with placebo for 2 years on the background of the same community lifestyle programme.

population.label: T4DM participants
inclusion_criteria: Impaired glucose tolerance or newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes by OGTT

exposures.frequency: at weeks 0 and 6, then every 3 months

canonical_statement: TRAVERSE enrolled 5246 men aged 45-80 years with total testosterone greater than 3.5 and at or below 10.4 nmol/L plus symptoms or signs of testosterone deficiency, and compared titrated testosterone gel with placebo for up to 4 years, with a mean treatment duration of about 22 months.

population.label: TRAVERSE participants
inclusion_criteria: Symptoms or signs of testosterone deficiency

canonical_statement: Across T-Trials and TRAVERSE, testosterone produced small improvements in vitality or mood, whereas TEAAM and T4DM did not show corresponding health-related quality-of-life benefits.

source_anchor.paragraph: Vitality/energy, mood, and cognitive function

canonical_statement: Testosterone did not produce a convincing overall improvement in cognitive function in the T-Trials cognitive substudy, TEAAM, or TRAVERSE; an exploratory executive-function signal in the full T-Trials cohort requires confirmation.

source_anchor.paragraph: Vitality/energy, mood, and cognitive function

canonical_statement: The authors conclude that average improvements in vitality and mood are too small to serve as the sole criterion for initiating testosterone therapy.

canonical_statement: In a secondary T-Trials analysis, testosterone reduced fasting insulin by an adjusted mean 1.7 µIU/mL compared with placebo (P=.02).
In a secondary T-Trials analysis, testosterone reduced HOMA-IR by an adjusted mean 0.6 compared with placebo (P=.03).
In T4DM, diabetes occurred in 55 of 443 testosterone-treated men (12.4%) and 87 of 413 placebo-treated men (21%), corresponding to a relative risk of 0.59 (95% CI 0.43-0.80; P=.0007).

canonical_statement: In the TRAVERSE diabetes substudy, testosterone did not significantly reduce progression from prediabetes to diabetes; the omnibus adjusted comparison was P=.49.

The authors hypothesize that testosterone may be more effective when used early in insulin-resistant men at high risk for type 2 diabetes than in men with longstanding diabetes and irreversible beta-cell dysfunction.

canonical_statement: In the T4DM bone substudy, testosterone increased lumbar-spine areal bone mineral density by 3.3% compared with placebo (95% CI 2.7-3.9; P<.001).

canonical_statement: In TRAVERSE, overall clinical fractures occurred in 91 of 2601 testosterone-treated men (3.50%) and 64 of 2603 placebo-treated men (2.46%), with ankle and rib fractures accounting for much of the excess.

source_anchor.paragraph: Effects of testosterone therapy on bone health

canonical_statement: The authors recommend that men at high risk of fragility fracture receive a therapy with proven anti-fracture benefit independently of decisions about testosterone therapy.

canonical_statement: Among T-Trials men with unexplained anemia, hemoglobin increased by at least 1.0 g/dL in 54% of testosterone-treated men versus 15% of placebo-treated men; the adjusted mean hemoglobin difference was 0.82 g/dL (95% CI 0.48-1.39; P=.002).

source_anchor.paragraph: Effect of testosterone therapy on haematologic parameters

canonical_statement: In TRAVERSE, anemia resolution was 41.0% with testosterone versus 27.5% with placebo at 6 months and 44.6% versus 39.2% at 48 months (P<.05).

source_anchor.paragraph: Effect of testosterone therapy on haematologic parameters

canonical_statement: In T4DM, erythrocytosis occurred in 22% of testosterone-treated men and 1% of placebo-treated men, and 0.5% of testosterone-treated men stopped therapy because of erythrocytosis.

source_anchor.paragraph: Effect of testosterone therapy on haematologic parameters

canonical_statement: The review notes that persistent clinically significant erythrocytosis was uncommon with transdermal regimens but substantially more frequent with the long-acting intramuscular regimen used in T4DM.

canonical_statement: In TRAVERSE, the primary MACE outcome occurred in 7.0% of testosterone-treated men and 7.3% of placebo-treated men, meeting the prespecified noninferiority criterion (P<.001 for noninferiority).

canonical_statement: In TRAVERSE, nonfatal arrhythmias requiring intervention occurred in 5.2% of testosterone-treated men versus 3.3% of placebo-treated men (P=.001).

source_anchor.paragraph: Effects of testosterone therapy on cardiovascular health

canonical_statement: In TRAVERSE, venous thromboembolism occurred in 1.7% of testosterone-treated men and 1.2% of placebo-treated men (hazard ratio 1.46, 95% CI 0.92-2.32).

source_anchor.paragraph: Effects of testosterone therapy on cardiovascular health

canonical_statement: In TRAVERSE, pulmonary embolism occurred in 24 testosterone-treated men versus 12 placebo-treated men; the low event count precluded formal significance testing.
TRAVERSE had treatment discontinuation rates of 61.4% in the testosterone group and 61.7% in the placebo group, limiting interpretation despite adequate power for short-term cardiovascular safety.

source_anchor.paragraph: Effects of testosterone therapy on cardiovascular health

canonical_statement: The authors conclude that the four major trials make a substantial short-term increase or decrease in major cardiovascular events unlikely, but arrhythmia and pulmonary-embolism signals warrant further study and individualized risk consideration.

source_anchor.paragraph: Effects of testosterone therapy on cardiovascular health

canonical_statement: In TEAAM, PSA increased more with testosterone than placebo, with a model-estimated mean difference of 0.28 ng/mL (95% CI 0.06-0.49; P=.01).

source_anchor.paragraph: Effects of testosterone therapy on prostate health

canonical_statement: In the T-Trials, 1.9% of testosterone-treated men and 0.3% of placebo-treated men had PSA at or above 4.0 ng/mL after 12 months.

source_anchor.paragraph: Effects of testosterone therapy on prostate health

canonical_statement: In TRAVERSE, mean PSA change from baseline was 0.20 ng/mL with testosterone versus 0.08 ng/mL with placebo (P<.001).

source_anchor.paragraph: Effects of testosterone therapy on prostate health

canonical_statement: In TRAVERSE, prostate cancer occurred in 12 testosterone-treated men (0.5%) and 11 placebo-treated men (0.4%; P=.87).

In TRAVERSE, incident BPH with lower urinary tract symptoms was similar with testosterone and placebo (45 vs 46; P=.92), while urinary retention showed a nonsignificant numerical excess (50 vs 34; P=.08).

canonical_statement: Across the prostate analyses, men at high prostate-cancer risk and men with severe BPH/LUTS were excluded, and prostate biopsies were not equally and systematically performed between treatment groups.

source_anchor.paragraph: Effects of testosterone therapy on prostate health

canonical_statement: The authors conclude that short-term trial data do not indicate increased de novo prostate cancer or BPH with LUTS, but testosterone raises PSA and may increase prostate-cancer evaluation and urinary-retention risk in susceptible men.

source_anchor.paragraph: Effects of testosterone therapy on prostate health

canonical_statement: The review supports personalized decision-making in middle-aged and older men without identifiable HPT-axis pathology by matching testosterone therapy to specific plausible benefits and counseling on small but relevant adverse-risk signals.

source_anchor.paragraph: Conclusions and outlook

canonical_statement: All four trials reviewed had treatment durations of 4 years or less, leaving longer-term cardiovascular and prostate outcomes unresolved.

source_anchor.paragraph: Conclusions and outlook

canonical_statement: The T-Trials coronary atheroma substudy had imbalanced baseline plaque volumes between testosterone and placebo groups, making the greater plaque-volume increase in testosterone-treated participants difficult to interpret.

source_anchor.paragraph: Conclusions and outlook

canonical_statement: The authors state that future research should address how testosterone affects healthy aging outcomes such as sustained independence and dementia and whether biomarkers can identify men most likely to benefit or be harmed.
